title: The Talmud and Jewish Life Through History
bigQuestion: How did a people who lost their Temple rebuild their religion around a book and an argument, and carry it through two thousand years of change?

story.title: Eight Lights or One?
story.kicker: In a synagogue study hall in Skokie, two students open a page of Talmud and find an argument that is two thousand years old and still going.
paragraphs: On a Tuesday night in a synagogue study hall in Skokie, the tables are covered with oversized books and the room is loud. No one asks for quiet. Pairs of students sit across from each other, reading aloud, pointing and interrupting. This way of learning has a name, chavruta, from an Aramaic word for companion. Ari and Sam, both seventeen, have been study partners since September. Tonight their teacher has assigned one page of the Babylonian Talmud: tractate Shabbat, page 21b.

The page looks like no page in a school textbook. In the center sits a block of large, square Hebrew letters. That is the core text, a short teaching followed by the discussion of later rabbis. Wrapped around it on the inner side is a column in a smaller, rounder script. That is the commentary of Rashi, who lived in France more than nine hundred years ago. On the outer side runs another column, the Tosafot, written by Rashi's grandsons and their students. Tiny notes and cross-references crowd the edges.

The subject is Hanukkah. Ari reads the passage aloud and Sam translates. The House of Shammai says to light eight lights on the first night and one fewer each night after. The House of Hillel says to light one on the first night and add one each night. Then the page gives reasons. One rabbi explains that Shammai's count matches the days still to come, and Hillel's the days already gone. Another says Hillel's rule follows a principle: in holy things you go up, not down.

Sam stops. We know who won, he says. Every family lights one candle on the first night now. So why does the page still print Shammai's side? Ari points to the inner column, where Rashi explains a phrase, and then to the outer column, where the Tosafot raise a question about Rashi's explanation. The losing view, the explanation and the question about the explanation all share one page. Nobody erased anything.

Their teacher, walking past, taps the page. You are sitting at a table with people who lived a thousand years apart, she says. The rabbis in the middle lived in Babylonia fifteen centuries ago. Rashi lived in France. The printers who fixed this layout worked in Venice and Vilna. Now two of you in Skokie are adding your own arguments. This chapter follows that long table: how a people who lost their Temple built a religion of study, and then carried it across the world.
story.think: Sam asks why the page keeps the losing side of the argument. What might a community gain by preserving opinions it decided not to follow?

lessons.title: The Second Temple Falls
lessons.mainIdea: In 70 CE Roman armies destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem, ending sacrifice and forcing Jewish life to find a new center.
reading: In Rome, near the ancient Forum, stands a stone arch built in the 80s CE to honor the emperor Titus. One carved panel shows soldiers carrying a great seven-branched lampstand, a *menorah*, as war loot. The scene records a real event. In 70 CE, Titus's legions captured Jerusalem and burned the Temple that stood at its heart. For many Jews in Rome over the centuries, the arch was a monument to loss, and some refused to walk beneath it.

That building is called the *Second Temple*. The first, built according to the Bible by King Solomon, was destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE. Exiles who returned from Babylon rebuilt it around 516 BCE, and King Herod greatly enlarged it shortly before the Common Era. For centuries it was the one place where priests offered the sacrifices the Torah commands. Pilgrims crowded the city for Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. Jewish groups of the period, such as the Sadducees, the Pharisees and the Essenes, disagreed about much, but the Temple stood at the center of their world.

In 66 CE a revolt broke out against Roman rule in Judea. Four years later the Temple lay in ruins. A second revolt, led by Simon bar Kokhba from 132 to 135 CE, also failed, and Rome barred Jews from Jerusalem. Only a retaining wall of the Temple platform survived. Today that *Western Wall* is the most visited Jewish holy site, where people pray and tuck written prayers into the cracks. Jewish tradition mourns both Temples on *Tisha B'Av*, the ninth day of the month of Av. It is a fast day on which the Book of Lamentations is read aloud.

words.d: a seven-branched lampstand that stood in the Temple; also the eight-branched Hanukkah lamp
the Temple in Jerusalem rebuilt around 516 BCE after the Babylonian exile and destroyed by Rome in 70 CE
a surviving retaining wall of the Temple platform in Jerusalem, now a place of Jewish prayer
the ninth of the month of Av, a fast day mourning the destruction of both Temples

look.title: A Lament for a City
look.text: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
look.prompt: Lamentations was written about the first destruction, in 586 BCE, yet it is read every Tisha B'Av for both Temples. Why might a community read an old lament for a newer loss?

check.q: What event does the carved panel on the Arch of Titus record?
choices: The Maccabees rededicating the Temple
Roman soldiers carrying off the Temple menorah after Jerusalem fell in 70 CE
King Solomon building the First Temple
The Babylonian exile of 586 BCE
check.why: The arch honors Titus, whose legions took Jerusalem and burned the Second Temple in 70 CE; the panel shows the menorah taken as loot.

check.q: What is the Western Wall?
choices: A wall Rome built to keep Jews out of Jerusalem
The last standing wall of the Temple's inner sanctuary
Part of King Solomon's palace
A surviving retaining wall of the Temple platform, now a place of prayer
check.why: The reading says only a retaining wall of the Temple platform survived. It is not a wall of the sanctuary building itself.

check.q: On Tisha B'Av, Jews fast and read which book of the Bible?
choices: Esther
Ruth
Lamentations
Psalms
check.why: Tisha B'Av mourns the destruction of both Temples, and the Book of Lamentations, a lament for Jerusalem, is read.

lessons.title: From Altar to Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: After 70 CE, rabbis at Yavneh rebuilt Jewish life around prayer, study and acts of kindness in place of Temple sacrifice.
reading: A famous rabbinic story tells how a teacher named Yohanan ben Zakkai escaped Jerusalem during the Roman siege. His students, the story says, carried him past the guards in a coffin. Brought before the Roman general Vespasian, he asked for one thing: give me Yavneh and its sages. Historians cannot confirm the details, but the story captures something real. After 70 CE, the town of *Yavneh*, near the coast, became the place where scholars began to rebuild Jewish life without a Temple.

Each of these teachers was called *rabbi*, meaning my teacher, and most historians see them as heirs of the Pharisees. They faced a hard question. The Torah commands sacrifices at the Temple, and the Temple was gone. Another story tells of Yohanan ben Zakkai walking past the ruins with a student who wept that the place of atonement was destroyed. Do not grieve, the teacher answered. We have another atonement just as good: acts of loving-kindness. Then he quoted the prophet Hosea.

Over the next generations the rabbis set daily prayer services at the hours when offerings had once been made. They fixed the core prayer, the *Amidah*, which means standing, since it is said on one's feet. They placed study of the Torah beside prayer as a way to draw near to God. The synagogue, which already existed in many towns, became the center of every community. Scholars call this new shape *rabbinic Judaism*. Nearly all Jewish movements today descend from it, and its mark is on the Sabbath table, the seder and the study hall.

words.d: a town near the Mediterranean coast where rabbis gathered to rebuild Jewish life after 70 CE
a Jewish teacher and scholar of Torah and Jewish law; the word means my teacher
the central Jewish prayer, said standing, at each daily service
the form of Judaism built by the rabbis after 70 CE around prayer, study and law, from which most Jewish movements descend

look.title: The Prophet's Answer
look.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
look.prompt: Hosea spoke centuries before 70 CE, while the Temple still stood. How could the rabbis use his words to answer a problem he never faced?

check.q: According to the rabbinic story, what did Yohanan ben Zakkai ask of the Roman general?
choices: Yavneh and its sages
That the Temple be spared
Permission to lead a new revolt
A ship to carry the Torah scrolls to Babylon
check.why: In the story he asks for Yavneh and its sages, a place to keep teaching, which became the center for rebuilding Jewish life.

check.q: What did the rabbis put in place of Temple sacrifice?
choices: Nothing; they waited for the Temple to be rebuilt before worshiping
Sacrifices at local altars in each town
Daily prayer at the hours of the old offerings, Torah study and acts of kindness
A new temple built at Yavneh
check.why: The reading says the rabbis set prayer at the hours of the offerings and placed study and loving-kindness beside it, citing Hosea.

check.q: The term rabbinic Judaism refers to:
choices: the religion of the priests who ran the Temple
a modern movement founded in the 1800s
the community of the Essenes near the Dead Sea
the form of Judaism the rabbis built after 70 CE, from which most Jewish movements descend
check.why: Rabbinic Judaism is the prayer-, study- and law-centered Judaism shaped by the rabbis after the Temple fell.

lessons.title: The Mishnah: Oral Torah in Writing
lessons.mainIdea: Around 200 CE, Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered the Oral Torah into the Mishnah, a Hebrew law code in six orders.
reading: A short tractate called Pirkei Avot, Ethics of the Fathers, opens with a chain of names. Moses received the Torah at Sinai and passed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Great Assembly. The list continues down to the early rabbis. The chain expresses a belief central to traditional Judaism. Along with the written Torah, God gave Moses an *Oral Torah*: explanations and laws handed down by word of mouth, from teacher to student.

The Oral Torah explains what the written text leaves open. The Torah says to rest on the Sabbath, and the oral tradition lists the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work. The Torah says to bind words on the hand, and the oral tradition explains how tefillin are made. For centuries this teaching was memorized and debated, not written down. After the Temple fell and the revolts failed, many feared it would be lost. Around 200 CE, in the Galilee, a leader known as *Rabbi Judah the Prince* edited these teachings into one book, the *Mishnah*, meaning repetition or teaching.

The Mishnah is written in compact Hebrew. It is divided into six orders, which cover farming and blessings, the Sabbath and festivals, marriage and family, civil and criminal law, the Temple and its offerings, and ritual purity. The orders hold sixty-three tractates, each on one subject. The teachers quoted in it are called the *Tannaim*, the repeaters. The Mishnah often records more than one opinion and names who held each. Traditional Jews regard it as the authoritative written form of the Oral Torah. Historians see it as the work of generations of scholars, gathered and shaped by its editor.

words.d: in traditional Jewish belief, the explanations and laws given with the written Torah and passed down by word of mouth
the leader of the Jewish community in the Galilee who edited the Mishnah around 200 CE
the first written collection of the Oral Torah, a Hebrew law code in six orders, completed around 200 CE
the rabbis whose teachings are recorded in the Mishnah; the word means repeaters

look.title: A Chain of Teachers
look.text: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets handed it to the men of the Great Assembly. They taught three things: be careful in judging, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah.
look.prompt: Why would a collection of rabbinic teaching begin with a chain of teachers reaching back to Moses? What does the chain claim about the rabbis' authority?

check.q: In traditional Jewish belief, what is the Oral Torah?
choices: A second set of stone tablets given at Sinai
Explanations and laws given with the written Torah and passed down by word of mouth
The Hebrew prayers read aloud in the synagogue
Family stories that are not considered sacred
check.why: The reading defines the Oral Torah as explanations and laws that tradition says God gave Moses alongside the written Torah, handed down teacher to student.

check.q: Who edited the Mishnah, and about when?
choices: Moses, at Sinai
Rashi, around 1100 CE
Maimonides, around 1180 CE
Rabbi Judah the Prince, around 200 CE
check.why: Rabbi Judah the Prince edited the Mishnah in the Galilee around 200 CE, when many feared the oral teachings would be lost.

check.q: What does the chain of names at the start of Pirkei Avot claim?
choices: That the rabbis' teaching goes back through an unbroken line of teachers to Moses at Sinai
That the Temple priests wrote the Torah
That each generation writes a new Torah
That the prophets rejected the elders
check.why: Pirkei Avot 1:1 traces the tradition from Moses to Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Great Assembly, linking the rabbis to Sinai.

lessons.title: What the Talmud Is
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud joins the Mishnah to centuries of rabbinic discussion called the Gemara, and it became the central text of Jewish study and law.
reading: Open any page of the Talmud and you will see a few lines of the Mishnah followed by a much longer passage marked *Gemara*, meaning study or completion. The Gemara records how later rabbis questioned, tested and applied the Mishnah over roughly three hundred years. Together, Mishnah and Gemara make up the *Talmud*, from a Hebrew word for learning. The Gemara is written mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in the Near East at that time.

There are two Talmuds. The Jerusalem Talmud, finished in the Galilee around 400 CE, is shorter. The Babylonian Talmud was produced in the academies of Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, and took its final form over the next two centuries. Babylonia had a large and stable Jewish community, and its Talmud is fuller. It became the one studied and followed most widely. When Jews today say the Talmud without a label, they mean the Babylonian. Its standard printed edition fills about 2,700 double-sided pages.

The Talmud mixes two kinds of material. Much of it is law, debating everything from Sabbath rules to damage caused by an ox. The rest is *aggadah*, meaning telling: legends, sayings, advice, history and dreams. A legal debate may pause for a story about a rabbi and then return to the case. The goal is less to hand down a verdict than to train a way of reasoning. Since 1923 Jews around the world have followed *Daf Yomi*, a program of studying one page a day. The whole Talmud takes about seven and a half years, and the completion in 2020 filled a stadium in New Jersey with about ninety thousand people.

words.d: the later rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah, mostly in Aramaic, that makes up most of the Talmud
the Mishnah together with the Gemara; the central text of rabbinic study and law
the story and teaching material in the Talmud and other rabbinic texts, as opposed to law
a worldwide program, begun in 1923, of studying one page of Talmud a day

look.title: The Talmud by the Numbers
look.cite: Standard Vilna edition of the Babylonian Talmud; Daf Yomi program since 1923
look.prompt: A student studies one double-sided page a day. Use the pages row to check the last row. Why might a whole community studying the same page each day matter?

check.q: What two parts make up the Talmud?
choices: The Torah and the Prophets
The Mishnah and the Gemara
The Shema and the Amidah
Rashi and the Tosafot
check.why: The Talmud is the Mishnah plus the Gemara, the later discussion of it. Rashi and the Tosafot are commentaries printed around it.

check.q: Why did the Babylonian Talmud become the one most widely studied?
choices: It was written in Hebrew rather than Aramaic
It was finished before the Jerusalem Talmud
It came from the academies of a large, stable community and is fuller
It contains no stories
check.why: The reading says Babylonia had a large, stable Jewish community and its Talmud is fuller, so it became the standard.

check.q: A Talmud passage tells a legend about a rabbi caught in a storm at sea. What kind of material is this?
choices: Aggadah
Gemara law
Mishnah
Daf Yomi
check.why: Aggadah is the story and teaching material in the Talmud, as opposed to legal debate.

lessons.title: Hillel, Shammai and Holy Argument
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud preserves disagreement on purpose, and the debates of Hillel and Shammai show that argument for the sake of heaven is itself honored.
reading: Around the turn of the Common Era, two teachers led rival schools in Jerusalem. *Hillel*, remembered as patient and humble, and *Shammai*, remembered as strict and exacting, disagreed on many questions. Their students carried the debates on as the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai. The Hanukkah lights are one example: eight lights going down, or one light going up. In most of their disputes Jewish law follows Hillel, but the Talmud keeps Shammai's opinions and reasons.

The Talmud explains why. It says the two schools argued for three years, each claiming the law followed it. Then a heavenly voice declared: these and these are the words of the living God, but the law follows the House of Hillel. Why Hillel? Because, the Talmud says, its members were kind and modest. They taught Shammai's view along with their own and even mentioned it first. The lesson for readers is that a view can be set aside in practice and still be honored as part of the conversation.

Pirkei Avot gives a test for good disagreement. An argument *for the sake of heaven*, it says, will last; one that is not will not. Its example of the first kind is Hillel and Shammai. Its example of the second is Korah, who in the Book of Numbers rebels against Moses to win power for himself. This value runs through Jewish learning. Students often study in pairs, called *chavruta*, so that each can challenge the other. Rabbis still write rulings that name the opinions they did not follow, and a joke heard in study halls says: two Jews, three opinions.

words.d: a leading sage in Jerusalem around the turn of the Common Era, remembered for patience; Jewish law usually follows his school
Hillel's contemporary and rival, remembered as strict; the Talmud records his school's views and reasons
in Pirkei Avot, an argument pursued to find the truth rather than to win power or glory
a pair of study partners who read and argue over a text together

look.title: The Whole Torah on One Foot
look.text: A man came to Shammai and said: Convert me, on condition that you teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with a builder's measuring stick. The man went to Hillel, who accepted him and said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it.
look.prompt: Hillel sums up the Torah in one sentence and then adds go and learn it. Why add those last words? What does the story show about the two teachers' styles?

check.q: In the dispute over Hanukkah lights, what did the House of Hillel teach?
choices: Light eight on the first night and one fewer each night
Light one on the first night and add one each night
Light all eight lights every night
Light only on the first and last nights
check.why: Hillel's school taught adding one light each night, because in holy things one goes up, not down. Shammai's taught counting down from eight.

check.q: According to the Talmud, why does the law usually follow the House of Hillel?
choices: Hillel's school was larger and won a vote
Shammai's school left Jerusalem
Its members were kind and modest and taught Shammai's view along with their own
Hillel was a descendant of Moses
check.why: The Talmud says both views are words of the living God, but the law follows Hillel's school because its members were kind, modest and quoted Shammai first.

check.q: In Pirkei Avot, which is the example of an argument NOT for the sake of heaven?
choices: Hillel and Shammai
Yohanan ben Zakkai and Vespasian
The rabbis at Yavneh
Korah's rebellion against Moses
check.why: Pirkei Avot contrasts Hillel and Shammai, who argued for the truth, with Korah, who rebelled against Moses for his own power.

lessons.title: Commentaries, Codes and Print
lessons.mainIdea: Later scholars such as Rashi and Maimonides explained the Talmud and organized its law, and printing fixed the page students still use.
reading: In the town of Troyes, in northern France, a scholar named Shlomo Yitzhaki wrote short, clear notes on almost every line of the Bible and the Talmud. Jews know him by his initials as *Rashi* (1040 to 1105). His comments define hard words, sometimes in Old French, and fill in steps the Talmud skips. Rashi's grandsons and their students, known as the *Tosafot*, meaning additions, went further. They raised questions and compared passages across the whole Talmud. Their comments became the two columns that frame the center of every page.

Others wanted a clear answer to what the law actually requires. *Maimonides* (1138 to 1204), born in Córdoba in Muslim Spain, completed the Mishneh Torah around 1180. It arranged all of Jewish law by subject in fourteen books. In the 1500s Joseph Karo, working in Safed in the land of Israel, wrote the *Shulchan Arukh*, meaning set table, a practical guide based on Sephardi practice. Moses Isserles of Kraków, in Poland, added notes for Ashkenazi custom. Together they remain a standard reference for Orthodox Jewish law today.

Printing gave the page its shape. Between 1520 and 1523 Daniel Bomberg, a Christian printer in Venice, published the complete Babylonian Talmud with Rashi and the Tosafot around the text. His page numbers are still used, which is why a student anywhere can turn to Shabbat 21b. An edition printed in Vilna, Lithuania, in the 1880s added more commentaries and became the standard. Not every ruler welcomed the book. In Paris in 1242, after a public disputation put the Talmud on trial, officials burned thousands of handwritten volumes. That is one reason early manuscripts are rare.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki (1040–1105) of Troyes, France, whose commentary explains the Bible and Talmud line by line
comments by Rashi's grandsons and students that question and compare passages; printed on the outer column of a Talmud page
Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), philosopher, physician and author of the Mishneh Torah, a code of Jewish law
a practical code of Jewish law by Joseph Karo, printed in 1565, with notes on Ashkenazi custom by Moses Isserles

look.title: Reading the Layout
look.text: Picture a page of the Vilna Talmud. In the center: a few lines of Mishnah in square letters, then the Gemara. On the inner column, toward the binding: Rashi's notes in a smaller, rounded script. On the outer column: the Tosafot, often longer and full of questions. Around the edges: references to Bible verses, to the codes of Maimonides and the Shulchan Arukh, and to other pages of the Talmud.
look.prompt: Using the reading, put these voices in order from earliest to latest: the Tosafot, the Mishnah, the Gemara, Rashi. What does the layout suggest about how Jewish tradition treats earlier and later voices?

check.q: Where did Rashi live, and what did he write?
choices: Troyes, France; short notes explaining the Bible and Talmud
Córdoba, Spain; a law code in fourteen books
Safed; the Shulchan Arukh
Venice; the first complete printed Talmud
check.why: Rashi lived in Troyes in northern France and wrote clear line-by-line notes on the Bible and Talmud.

check.q: What was the purpose of codes like the Mishneh Torah and the Shulchan Arukh?
choices: To replace the written Torah
To add new legends to the aggadah
To arrange the law by subject so readers could find what to do
To translate the Talmud into French
check.why: Maimonides and Joseph Karo organized Jewish law by subject to give clear, usable answers about practice.

check.q: Why can students anywhere find the same passage by citing Shabbat 21b?
choices: The Talmud has only ever been printed in one city
Rashi numbered the pages himself
The Mishnah has sixty-three tractates
The page numbers set by the Venice printing of 1520 to 1523 are still used
check.why: Daniel Bomberg's Venice edition fixed the page numbering, and later editions such as Vilna kept it.

lessons.title: Sepharad and Ashkenaz
lessons.mainIdea: Jews under Islamic rule and in Christian Europe formed two great cultural families, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, with different languages and customs.
reading: Medieval Jews borrowed two place names from the Bible to describe where they lived. *Sepharad* came to mean Spain, and *Ashkenaz* came to mean the German lands along the Rhine. Sephardi Jews trace their roots to Spain and Portugal, and many spoke Ladino, a form of Spanish often written in Hebrew letters. Ashkenazi Jews spread from Germany into Central and Eastern Europe and spoke Yiddish, a German-based language with Hebrew and Slavic words. Jews of the Middle East and North Africa, from Iraq, Iran, Yemen and Morocco, are often called *Mizrahi*, from the Hebrew for eastern.

For centuries most of the world's Jews lived under Muslim rule. Islamic law classed Jews and Christians as *dhimmi*, protected peoples of scripture. They could practice their religion and run their own courts, but they paid a special tax and faced limits, such as rules against building new houses of worship in some places. Conditions varied by ruler and century. In al-Andalus, as Muslim Spain was called, Jewish poets, doctors and scholars flourished from the 900s to the 1100s. Samuel ibn Naghrela served as chief minister of Granada. In Baghdad, the scholar Saadia Gaon translated the Torah into Arabic.

Protection could also break down. In the 1140s the Almohads, a strict dynasty from North Africa, took control of much of Muslim Spain and pressed Jews and Christians to convert. The family of the young Maimonides fled, eventually settling in Egypt. There he became a court physician in Cairo and a leader of its Jewish community, and he wrote his philosophy in Arabic. His life, moving from Spain to Morocco to Egypt, shows both the richness of Jewish life under Islam and its insecurity. Historians still debate how to weigh the tolerance and the limits of that age.

words.d: the medieval Hebrew name for Spain; Sephardi Jews trace their roots to Spain and Portugal
the medieval Hebrew name for the German lands; Ashkenazi Jews trace their roots to Central and Eastern Europe
Jews whose families come from the Middle East and North Africa, such as Iraq, Iran, Yemen and Morocco
under Islamic law, the protected status of Jews and Christians, with freedom of worship, a special tax and some limits

look.title: Two Seders, One Story
look.text: At a Sephardi Passover seder in Chicago, the family eats rice and chickpeas alongside the matzah and sings a song in Ladino. At an Ashkenazi seder across town, rice and beans are avoided, the soup has matzah balls, and a grandparent sings a verse in Yiddish. Both families read the Haggadah in Hebrew, and both tell the story of the exodus from Egypt.
look.prompt: What is shared and what differs between the two tables? Using the reading, explain where each family's customs and languages might have come from.

check.q: In medieval Jewish usage, Sepharad and Ashkenaz referred to:
choices: Babylon and Jerusalem
Spain and the German lands
Egypt and Persia
Poland and Italy
check.why: Medieval Jews used the biblical names Sepharad for Spain and Ashkenaz for the German lands along the Rhine.

check.q: What was dhimmi status under Islamic rule?
choices: Forced conversion to Islam
Full equality with Muslims in every law
Protected status for peoples of scripture, with freedom of worship, a special tax and some limits
A ban on Jews living in cities
check.why: Dhimmi status protected Jews and Christians and let them keep their religion and courts, but with a special tax and restrictions.

check.q: Yiddish and Ladino are:
choices: two names for Hebrew
prayer books of the Reform movement
Jewish languages based on Arabic and Greek
Jewish languages based on German and Spanish
check.why: Yiddish, spoken by Ashkenazi Jews, is German-based; Ladino, spoken by many Sephardi Jews, is Spanish-based.

lessons.title: Expulsions, Ghettos and the Shtetl
lessons.mainIdea: In medieval Christian Europe, Jews faced violence, false accusations and expulsions, and many moved east to Poland, where Jewish life grew and Hasidism began.
reading: In 1096, bands on their way to the First Crusade attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland towns of Speyer, Worms and Mainz. Many hundreds were killed, and some chose death over forced baptism. Jewish chroniclers wrote down the names, and prayers remembering the dead are still said. Over the next centuries false charges led to more massacres. One was the *blood libel*, the invented claim that Jews killed Christian children for ritual use, first recorded in Norwich, England, in 1144. During the Black Death, around 1348, Jews were falsely blamed for poisoning wells.

Church and rulers also set legal limits. A church council in 1215 required Jews and Muslims to wear distinctive clothing. Jews were often barred from owning land or joining craft guilds, which pushed many into trade and moneylending. Then came *expulsion*, the forced removal of a whole community. England expelled its Jews in 1290 and France in 1306. In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella ordered all Jews in Spain who would not convert to leave, and in 1497 Portugal forced most of its Jews to convert. Many Sephardi exiles found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, North Africa and later Amsterdam.

In 1516 the city of Venice required its Jews to live on a small island beside an old foundry, called a getto in the local dialect, whose gates were locked at night. The word *ghetto* spread across Europe for closed Jewish quarters. Meanwhile many Ashkenazi Jews moved east to Poland and Lithuania, where kings invited them and granted charters. By the 1700s this region held the largest Jewish population in the world, much of it in small market towns, each called a *shtetl* in Yiddish. There, in the mid-1700s, a teacher known as the Baal Shem Tov inspired *Hasidism*, a movement stressing joyful prayer and heartfelt devotion, not scholarship alone.

words.d: the false and deadly accusation that Jews killed Christian children for ritual purposes
the forced removal of a whole community from a country or city
a closed quarter where Jews were required to live, named after the Jewish quarter of Venice created in 1516
a small Eastern European market town with a large Jewish population; Yiddish for little town
a Jewish movement begun in Eastern Europe in the 1700s that stresses joyful prayer, devotion and loyalty to a rebbe

look.title: When Communities Were Uprooted
look.prompt: How many years separate the expulsion from England and the expulsion from Spain? According to the reading, where did the exiles from Spain find refuge?

check.q: What was the blood libel?
choices: A church law requiring distinctive clothing
A tax paid by Jews under Islamic rule
A false accusation that Jews killed Christian children for ritual use
A Talmudic law about kosher slaughter
check.why: The blood libel was an invented charge, first recorded in Norwich in 1144, that led to attacks on Jewish communities.

lessons.title: Citizenship and the Movements
lessons.mainIdea: As European Jews gained citizenship in the 1700s and 1800s, they answered modern life differently, forming the Reform, Orthodox, Conservative and Reconstructionist movements.
reading: In 1783 Moses Mendelssohn, a Jewish philosopher in Berlin, finished a translation of the Torah into German, printed in Hebrew letters. Jews could learn the language of their neighbors through their own sacred text. Mendelssohn became a symbol of the *Haskalah*, the Jewish Enlightenment, which urged Jews to study science and European languages alongside Torah. At the same time came *emancipation*, the granting of equal citizenship. France was first, in 1791, and other countries followed slowly. For the first time Jews could enter universities, professions and politics, and each had to decide what Jewish life should look like.

Reform Judaism began in Germany in the early 1800s. Its founders shortened services, added prayers and sermons in German and organ music, and taught that Jewish law should change with the times while its ethical core stayed. In the United States, Isaac Mayer Wise founded Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati in 1875 to train Reform rabbis. In response, leaders who held that the Torah and halakhah are unchanging divine law came to be called Orthodox. Samson Raphael Hirsch in Germany taught that faithful Jews could keep the whole law and also take part in modern culture.

Others sought a middle path. Conservative Judaism, rooted in the work of Zacharias Frankel in Germany, held that Jewish law is binding but has always developed through history. In America it grew around the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York, founded in 1886. In the twentieth century Rabbi Mordecai Kaplan described Judaism as an evolving religious civilization, and his followers founded *Reconstructionist* Judaism. In Eastern Europe and later in America and Israel, Hasidic groups kept their own path under a rebbe. Each *denomination*, or organized movement, differs on law, worship and the roles of women and men. Yet most Jews recognize one another as one people.

words.d: the Jewish Enlightenment of the 1700s and 1800s, which urged Jews to study science and European languages alongside Torah
the granting of equal citizenship and legal rights to Jews, beginning in France in 1791
the Jewish movement founded on Mordecai Kaplan's idea of Judaism as an evolving religious civilization
an organized movement within a religion, such as Reform, Conservative or Orthodox Judaism

lessons.title: The Holocaust
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1933 and 1945 Nazi Germany carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of about six million Jews, which Jews also call the Shoah.
reading: At the Illinois Holocaust Museum in Skokie, visitors pass a German railroad car of the kind used to deport Jews to killing centers. The museum was founded by survivors who had made new lives in Skokie. In 1977 and 1978, when a neo-Nazi group sought to march in their village, many decided they had to tell their stories in public. The event they described is called the *Holocaust*, from a Greek word for a sacrifice burned whole. Many Jews prefer the Hebrew word *Shoah*, meaning catastrophe.

The Nazi Party took power in Germany in 1933 and quickly pushed Jews out of public life. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped German Jews of citizenship. On November 9 and 10, 1938, in attacks called *Kristallnacht*, mobs burned synagogues and smashed Jewish shops across Germany and Austria. After World War II began in 1939, Jews in occupied Europe were forced into sealed ghettos. From 1941 mobile killing units shot Jews by the hundreds of thousands, and the regime built killing centers such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka. About six million Jews were murdered, roughly two of every three Jews in Europe, including as many as 1.5 million children.

The Nazis also persecuted and murdered Roma, disabled people, Polish and Soviet civilians and prisoners of war, gay men and others. Jews resisted in many ways, from the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 to secret schools and hidden prayer. After the war, Jewish thinkers responded in different ways. Some asked how to speak of God at all. Others insisted that continuing Jewish life was itself the answer. Jewish communities mark *Yom HaShoah*, Holocaust Remembrance Day, each spring. In 1990, Illinois became the first state to require public schools to teach about the Holocaust.

words.d: the systematic, state-sponsored murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, 1933 to 1945
the Hebrew word, meaning catastrophe, that many Jews use for the Holocaust
the attacks of November 9 and 10, 1938, when mobs burned synagogues and wrecked Jewish shops in Germany and Austria
Holocaust Remembrance Day, observed by Jewish communities each spring

Decades later, the museum they helped found records their testimony so that students can still hear it after the survivors are gone.

lessons.title: Israel and the Diaspora
lessons.mainIdea: Modern Zionism led to the founding of Israel in 1948; today nearly half of the world's Jews live there and the rest in the diaspora, with a wide range of views.
reading: At many Jewish weddings, before the glass is broken, someone recites a line from Psalm 137, written after the Babylonian exile: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning. For centuries Jews living far away faced Jerusalem in prayer and ended the Passover seder with the words next year in Jerusalem. Jews use the word *diaspora*, a Greek term for scattering, for Jewish communities outside the land of Israel. For most of that history, the hope of return was a religious hope, left to God's timing.

In the late 1800s, amid rising nationalism and violent attacks on Jews in Eastern Europe, a political movement called *Zionism* argued that Jews needed a state of their own. Theodor Herzl, a journalist in Vienna, organized the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, in 1897. Jewish immigration to Ottoman and then British-ruled Palestine grew. After the Holocaust, the United Nations voted in 1947 to divide the land into a Jewish state and an Arab state. Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, and war with neighboring Arab states followed. About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes, which Palestinians call the Nakba, the catastrophe. In the following years hundreds of thousands of Jews left or were forced out of Arab countries, and many settled in Israel.

Jews have never agreed about Zionism. Early Reform leaders saw Judaism as a religion rather than a nation. Some *Haredi*, or strictly Orthodox, groups hold that only God should restore Jewish rule in the land. Over time most Jewish movements came to support the state. Israel's *Law of Return* (1950) gives any Jew the right to settle there and become a citizen. Many Jews distinguish between Judaism as a religion and the policies of Israel's government, which Israelis and Jews abroad debate sharply. The conflict between Israelis and Palestinians continues. Today nearly half of the world's Jews live in Israel, and the largest diaspora community is in the United States.

words.d: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel; from a Greek word for scattering
the movement, organized from the 1890s, to create and support a Jewish state in the land of Israel
strictly Orthodox Jews who keep a traditional way of life with limited involvement in secular culture
Israel's 1950 law giving any Jew the right to settle in Israel and become a citizen

lessons.title: Jewish Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 1840s Jewish immigrants have built congregations, markets and institutions in Chicago, moving from the Near West Side to the North Side and suburbs.
reading: Chicago's first Jewish *congregation*, Kehilath Anshe Maariv, the Congregation of the Men of the West, was founded in 1847 by immigrants from Germany. After later mergers it continues today as KAM Isaiah Israel in the Kenwood neighborhood. Chicago's German Jews built Reform congregations such as Chicago Sinai, founded in 1861. At the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions, Chicagoan Hannah Greenebaum Solomon organized a Jewish Women's Congress. Out of it grew the National Council of Jewish Women, which still works on social causes.

From the 1880s to the 1920s, tens of thousands of Jews from Eastern Europe arrived, fleeing poverty and violence. Many crowded into the Near West Side around Maxwell Street, whose open-air market sold everything from pickles to overcoats. They spoke Yiddish and founded small Orthodox synagogues. They also formed societies for people from the same hometown, each called a *landsmanshaft*, which helped members with loans, jobs and burial. Jane Addams's Hull House nearby served many of these families. As they prospered, many moved west to Lawndale, then north to Albany Park and Rogers Park, and later to suburbs such as Skokie and Highland Park.

Chicago Jews also built lasting institutions for the whole city. Julius Rosenwald, president of Sears, Roebuck, gave much of his fortune to *philanthropy*. He helped fund the Museum of Science and Industry and thousands of schools for Black children in the rural South, built together with local Black communities. Today the Chicago area is home to roughly 300,000 Jews, by common estimates, and every movement is present, from Orthodox families along Devon Avenue in West Rogers Park to Reform temples on the North Shore. Hebrew Theological College in Skokie trains Orthodox rabbis, and the Spertus Institute on Michigan Avenue offers Jewish learning to the public.

words.d: a community that gathers for worship, usually around one synagogue
a society of immigrants from the same European hometown that helped members with loans, jobs and burial
